A Garden Of Possibilities: Growing Ideas Into Impact At Xperience 2026

⤢

What happens when good ideas are given the space, support and people they need to grow? At Xperience 2026, MOE colleagues got to see the possibilities for themselves.

Xperience is DXD’s annual product showcase and launch event, bringing together digital solutions developed across MOE to address real needs in our schools and HQ. It is a chance for colleagues to discover what is possible, experience products first-hand and explore how digital innovation can make a difference to educators, students, parents and schools.

This year’s theme, A Garden of Possibilities, captures that journey. Like a garden, innovation begins with a seed, an idea sparked by a real need, and flourishes with the right conditions, collective effort and continuous nurturing.

On Wednesday, 11 November, MOE HQ became a garden of innovation, welcoming more than 400 attendees, with 156 schools represented. School Leaders and HQ colleagues explored 28 digital products, met the teams behind them and saw how these solutions could support their work. The products were organised around four themes: Empowering Educators, Growing Learners, Partnering Parents and Powering Schools.

Beyond the products, the event raised a bigger question: How do we turn technology into meaningful improvements in the way we teach, learn and work?

The keynote sessions offered five important perspectives.

1. Begin with the problem, not the technology

Ms Liew Wei Li reminded colleagues that digital transformation starts with clarity of purpose: identify the outcome you want, rethink how the work is done and simplify where possible.

💬 Ms Liew Wei Li

“Putting a digital tool to take over an inefficient process is just simply digitising the inefficiency.”

Technology should create opportunities to do things better, not simply replicate existing ways of working.

2. Put better learning experiences at the heart of innovation

Through examples such as LangBuddy, the Pre-U Economics Learning Assistant, Learning Journal and My World, Mr Jason See showed how digital tools and AI can support more personalised, self-directed learning. The aim is not to have technology think for students, but to help them think more deeply and take greater ownership of their learning.

💬 Mr Jason See

“It’s not just about better technology. It’s really about better experiences for our educators, our schools and our students.”

3. Give educators more time and better insights to focus on what matters

Technology can reduce fragmented workflows, repetitive tasks and administrative demands. Tools such as Teacher Workspace, Student Insights, Casing and Markly bring information together and support more informed decisions, complementing educators’ professional judgement and giving them more time for their students.

4. Grow better solutions by building them with educators

The school sharings showed how schools and HQ teams identify challenges, experiment and refine products based on actual needs. Bringing educators in from the start helps shape solutions that are practical and grounded in school life.

💬 Mr Jason See

The best solutions are those “built with educators”.

5. Turn products into impact by making them part of how we work

A launch is a milestone, not the finish line. Mrs Tan Chen Kee highlighted the “product-impact gap”, the distance between introducing a tool and seeing real improvements from its use. Closing it takes schools rethinking processes, embracing new mindsets and integrating tools into everyday practice.

💬 Mrs Tan Chen Kee

A product or tool “works when it becomes how we work.”

Growing possibilities, together

Behind every booth was a team that had invested time, creativity and energy in turning ideas into solutions, many working closely with schools and HQ colleagues to test, learn and improve. Meaningful innovation is never a solo endeavour. A garden does not flourish because of one seed or one gardener; it grows through many hands working together.

Xperience 2026 may have come to a close, but the possibilities it showcased continue to grow. The next step is to bring these ideas into our schools and workplaces and turn their potential into everyday impact.

Spotted a product you’d like to explore further, or have an idea for how digital solutions could support your school or division? Get in touch with the DXD team at MOE_DXD@moe.gov.sg. After all, the best possibilities are the ones we grow together.

Reminder: Your AIBots Bots Are Moving to Desk

⏰ Deadline: 31 October

If you're an AIBots user, what describes your bot? Tap one to see what to do.

Quick reminder: all active bots on AIBots will be migrated to Desk between November and December. If a bot has been used at least once in October, it is included. Take a minute this month to check yours.

Your checklist

  • Seasonal bot you still need: start at least one chat with it in October so it counts as active.
  • Active bot you do not want moved: delete it by 31 October.
  • New bot: do not create it on AIBots after 31 October. Create it directly on Desk as a Chat Assistant.

What happens to your bots

The migration creates a duplicate of your bot on Desk. Your original bot on AIBots is not deleted, and stays available until the migration has stabilised and users have transitioned smoothly to Desk.

We will keep you updated as the migration progresses. Thank you for your support as we make this transition to Desk.

03

A Smoother Xperience, One Less Task to Chase

400+invitations sent
~10 minsaved each working day
5 minbetween automatic checks for new sign-ups

How much time do we spend on tasks that are necessary, but repetitive? Sending emails, updating spreadsheets, tracking submissions and following up with people are all part of the workday. Individually, these tasks may take only a few minutes. But when repeated day after day, they can quietly add up — taking time and attention away from other priorities.

For Ameline from DIVA, managing registrations for Xperience 2026 was one such task. As participants signed up through FormSG, their details had to be downloaded, organised in a spreadsheet and checked against those who had already received calendar invitations. New participants then had to be sent invitations individually through Outlook, with the spreadsheet updated to keep track of who had been contacted.

It was a manageable process, but one that required regular attention. Each working day, about 10 minutes went into checking registrations and sending invitations. There was also the need to keep track of the latest sign-ups to avoid missing anyone or sending duplicate invitations.

Rather than continue with the same routine, Ameline began exploring whether the process could be made simpler. Inspired by an automated invitation workflow used for another event, she looked into how Power Automate could help streamline the registration process for Xperience.

Turning a repetitive task into a smoother workflow

The idea was simple: instead of manually checking for new registrations and sending each invitation, let an automated workflow handle the repetitive steps.

Using Power Automate, Ameline connected the registration data in Excel to a workflow that checked for new sign-ups every five minutes. When a new participant was detected, the workflow automatically sent a calendar invitation through Outlook and updated the spreadsheet to show that the invitation had been sent.

Before 📥 Download FormSG details› 📑 Update spreadsheet› 🔎 Check who has been invited› ✉️ Send each invite in Outlook
After 📝 Participant signs up› ⏱️ Power Automate checks every 5 min› 📅 Invite sent via Outlook› ✅ Spreadsheet updated

This meant participants could receive their invitations shortly after registering, without someone having to constantly monitor the registration list. The spreadsheet also became a useful reference for checking which participants had been invited.

Getting the workflow to run smoothly, however, took some experimentation. Early versions encountered a few hiccups, including repeated notifications and slower-than-expected processing. Instead of giving up, Ameline tested different approaches, used AI tools to help troubleshoot issues and refined the workflow along the way.

The result was a more reliable process that has since sent more than 400 invitations and saves about 10 minutes each working day. More importantly, it has reduced the need for repeated manual checks and given the team greater peace of mind that new registrations are being followed up.

Start with the task that keeps coming back

The value of this experience goes beyond automating calendar invitations. It shows that improving the way we work does not always require a major project, a technical background or an entirely new system. Sometimes, it starts with noticing a small frustration in our daily routine and being curious enough to explore a better way.

For officers looking to do the same, here are a few ways to get started:

1

Spot the repetitive tasks.

Look out for work that involves repeating the same steps regularly — such as sending reminders, consolidating information, updating trackers, copying data between spreadsheets or following up on submissions. These are often good places to start exploring improvements.

2

Understand the problem before choosing a tool.

Before jumping into a new application, take a moment to map out the existing process. What information needs to move from one place to another? Which steps are repeated? Where do delays or manual errors tend to happen? Understanding the process helps identify what can realistically be simplified or automated.

3

Start small and build on what you already have.

You don’t need to automate an entire process from the outset. Pick one repetitive step and explore whether tools already available to you, such as Power Automate or other approved digital tools, can help. A small improvement that works reliably is often more useful than an ambitious solution that is difficult to maintain.

4

Experiment, test and refine.

The first attempt may not work perfectly, and that’s part of the learning process. Test your solution with a small number of cases before using it more widely. Check that the results are accurate, consider what might go wrong, and make adjustments where needed. AI tools can also be useful sounding boards for understanding errors, exploring ideas and working through possible solutions.

5

Keep people in the loop.

Automation can take care of repetitive steps, but it does not replace human judgement. Continue checking that the process is working as intended, especially when it involves important information or communications. Think of automation as a way to support the work, not remove the need for oversight.

Small changes can make a difference

Ameline’s experience with Xperience 2026 is a reminder that digital transformation does not always begin with a big idea or a sophisticated solution. It can start with a simple question:

💬 Worth asking

Is there a better way to do something we do every day?

The next time a routine task feels unnecessarily repetitive, take a moment to look at the process. Could a step be simplified? Could information be brought together more easily? Could a reminder or update happen automatically?

You don’t have to have all the answers before getting started. Be curious, try something small, and learn along the way. One less task to chase may seem like a small win, but many small improvements can add up to a smoother and more productive workday.
